criteria.descriptor: Full marks: accurately describes both architectures and their coordination mechanism (single agentic loop/shared tools vs supervisor-routed specialized sub-agents with handoffs/shared state) and states trade-offs that are actually true -- e.g. multi-agent adds LLM round-trips, latency, and cost rather than reducing them. Deduct for wrong claims such as multi-agent being inherently cheaper/faster, or conflating the two designs.

Full marks: covers both definitions, at least one real advantage AND one real cost for each side (including the tool-overload failure mode and a handoff/observability concern), and a recommendation. Deduct for covering only one architecture, listing pros without cons, or omitting the recommendation.

Full marks: the recommendation follows from the trade-offs and is tied to this help-desk system's growing tool count and distinct domains (HR/provisioning/security), rather than a generic preference; shows judgement about when the single agent stops being adequate.

Full marks: well-organized and concise, using correct vocabulary (orchestrator/supervisor, sub-agent, handoff, tool-selection, context window) so a reviewer can follow the comparison and the recommendation easily.

expected_answer_points: Defines a single-agent system as one LLM iterating a reason/act/observe loop over a single context with a shared set of tools.
Defines a multi-agent system as an orchestrator/supervisor routing to specialized sub-agents that each have focused instructions/tools and coordinate via handoffs or shared state.
Names a genuine single-agent advantage (simplicity, single unbroken context, lower latency/cost from fewer LLM round-trips, or easier tracing/debugging).
Identifies the single-agent failure mode as scope grows: a large mixed tool set degrades tool-selection accuracy and the prompt/context becomes bloated with competing concerns.
Names a genuine multi-agent advantage (focused per-agent tools/instructions, isolated context per domain, or independent scaling/ownership).
Names a genuine multi-agent cost (coordination overhead, more LLM calls raising latency/cost, harder observability, or context loss / error propagation across handoffs).
Gives a justified recommendation for this scenario: default to the single agent and adopt multi-agent only when tool count/distinct domains justify it, decomposing along real domain boundaries.
common_pitfalls: Treats multi-agent as simply more advanced/better and recommends it by default, ignoring the added latency, token cost, and debugging burden it introduces.
Defines the two designs only superficially ('one bot vs several bots') without the mechanisms -- supervisor/routing, per-agent focused tool sets, handoffs or shared state.
Claims multi-agent is cheaper or faster because work is 'parallelized', when specialist routing typically adds sequential LLM round-trips and token overhead.
Ignores the actual driver of the decision -- that a single agent's tool-selection accuracy and prompt clarity degrade as the tool set grows.
Overlooks handoff-specific risks such as context/state loss between agents, error propagation, and reduced observability.
Gives no recommendation, or one not justified against this scenario's growing and genuinely distinct domains.
reference_answer:
A single-agent system is one LLM running an agentic loop over a single context and a shared tool set: it reasons, calls a tool, observes the result, and repeats until done. A multi-agent system decomposes the work across specialized agents -- typically an orchestrator/supervisor that routes each request to a sub-agent (an HR agent, a provisioning agent, a security-triage agent), each with its own focused instructions, tool set, and context, coordinating via handoffs or shared state.

Single-agent strengths: simpler to build and reason about; one context so nothing is lost between steps; lower latency and token cost because there are fewer model round-trips; and far easier to trace and debug. Its weakness is that it degrades as scope grows -- a large, mixed tool set hurts tool-selection accuracy, the system prompt bloats with competing instructions, and unrelated domains contend for the same context window.

Multi-agent strengths: each agent stays small and focused, so tool selection and instructions are cleaner; distinct domains are isolated; teams can build, scale, and own subsystems independently. Costs: coordination overhead, more LLM calls (higher latency and spend), harder observability, and the risk of context loss or error propagation across handoffs.

Recommendation: keep the single agent for now, perhaps grouping tools, and introduce a supervisor + sub-agents only once the growing tool count and genuinely distinct domains make one prompt unreliable. Don't add orchestration complexity before the single agent measurably breaks; when it does, decompose along the real domain boundaries (HR, provisioning, security).
